summary: Botswana lies in the interior of southern Africa, became independent from Britain in 1966, and is known for its stable democracy, its diamond industry and the wildlife of the Okavango Delta.

ranking.name: Protestantism (including African independent churches)
ranking.description: Protestantism was introduced in the early 19th century by the London Missionary Society of Britain; in 1841 the missionary Livingstone came to the Tswana region, and in 1848 he baptized Sechele, chief of the Bakwena. In 1885 Britain made the Botswana area the Bechuanaland Protectorate, and many Tswana chiefs converted to Christianity and took the church as an adviser, so that Protestantism spread rapidly. From the 20th century, African independent churches (such as the Zion Christian Church) grew rapidly, blending traditional healing with notions of ancestral spirits and attracting large numbers of followers.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The non-religious population is about 15%, mainly young people and the highly educated in cities. After independence in 1966 Botswana's economy developed quickly, the diamond industry drove urbanization, and the spread of education has led some people away from the church; some people in the census also do not identify with any religious organization but still retain traditional beliefs.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholicism was introduced in the late 19th century by German and Irish missionaries, but because the London Missionary Society had already built influence among the Tswana chiefs, Catholicism developed later. Today Catholics are mainly distributed in urban areas, and the schools and hospitals run by the church play a certain role in social services.

ranking.name: Traditional beliefs (Badimo)
ranking.description: Badimo is the traditional ancestral-spirit belief of the Tswana, holding that the spirits of ancestors can bless or punish living relatives, who communicate with them through sacrifices, divination and traditional healers. Although Christianity has become the mainstream, many people still keep Badimo customs at weddings and funerals, newborn naming and farming rituals.

religion.background: Before Christianity arrived, the Tswana believed in the creator god Modimo and the ancestral spirits Badimo, and chiefs also had a religious role. In the 19th century London Missionary Society missionaries such as Robert Moffat and Livingstone entered the area, and the conversion of tribal chiefs led to large-scale Christianization. From 1885 Britain ruled the Bechuanaland Protectorate, and the churches controlled most of the education. After independence in 1966, Botswana became a stable democracy, religious freedom was guaranteed, and African independent churches and Pentecostals have grown rapidly in recent decades.

language.official: English is the official language and Setswana is the national language.

ranking.name: Setswana
ranking.description: Setswana belongs to the Sotho–Tswana group of the Bantu languages and is the language of the Tswana, the country's largest ethnic group; the country's name 'Botswana' means 'land of the Tswana'. In the 19th century the London Missionary Society missionary Robert Moffat translated the Bible into Setswana (the complete Bible was finished in 1857), laying the foundation of the written language. After independence in 1966 Setswana was made the national language, about 77% of the population have it as their mother tongue, and other ethnic groups also commonly use it.

ranking.name: Kalanga
ranking.description: Kalanga is the language of the Kalanga people of the northeast, close to Zimbabwe's Shona, and the Kalanga are among the descendants of the inhabitants of the medieval Great Zimbabwe culture and the Torwa Kingdom (about 1450–1683), living mainly around Francistown. After independence the government pursued a single national-language policy of Setswana, and Kalanga was long left out of school education; only in recent years has there been a movement to promote mother-tongue teaching.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: English became the language of administration and education during the British Bechuanaland Protectorate of 1885–1966 and became the official language after independence. Because government, the courts, higher education and commerce all use English, most educated Batswana can speak English, but only about 3% have English as their mother tongue.

language.history: The earliest inhabitants of Botswana were the San (Bushmen), who speak click languages, and their languages are still used in the Kalahari Desert region. Around the year 1000, Bantu-speaking peoples migrated south into the area, and in the 17th–18th centuries the Tswana established several chiefdoms in present-day Botswana. In the 19th century British missionaries created a Latin-alphabet writing system for Setswana, and after British rule in 1885 English became the administrative language. After independence in 1966, English is the official language and Setswana the national language, but other minority languages have long been neglected in education.

ranking.name: Seswaa
ranking.description: Beef or mutton is stewed with salt in an iron pot for several hours until the meat is tender, then pounded with a wooden pestle into shreds, often eaten with maize porridge.
ranking.history: Seswaa is regarded as the national dish of Botswana and is traditionally cooked by men in large three-legged iron pots at weddings, funerals and important festivals. Cattle are a symbol of wealth and status in Tswana society, and bridewealth was once counted in cattle. At the Independence Day celebrations on September 30 (independence in 1966), seswaa is an indispensable dish, symbolizing togetherness and sharing.

ranking.name: Bogobe (porridge)
ranking.description: A thick, porridge-like staple made by cooking sorghum flour or maize flour with water, with a smooth texture, often eaten with seswaa or vegetables.
ranking.history: Sorghum is one of the oldest native grains of southern Africa, and in the dry climate around the Kalahari Desert it is more drought-tolerant than maize, so it is the traditional staple of the Tswana. Maize was introduced in large quantities only in the colonial period and gradually replaced sorghum in part. Today the porridges made from both grains are commonly eaten in Botswana and are the basic staple of the everyday table.

ranking.name: Phane (mopane worms)
ranking.description: Large caterpillars from mopane trees are gutted, boiled and sun-dried, and can be eaten directly as a snack or stewed with tomato and onion, rich in protein.
ranking.history: Mopane worms are the larvae of the emperor moth and live on mopane trees; they have been a traditional food of southern Africa for hundreds of years, gathered by both the San and the Bantu peoples. In the gathering season after the rains each year, rural women gather them collectively and sell them dried, making them an important source of income. Because of their high protein content and ease of storage, they are also regarded as an important food for coping with drought and food shortages.

ranking.name: Morogo (wild greens)
ranking.description: Mainly wild leafy greens such as amaranth and cowpea leaves, stir-fried or stewed with onion and tomato, soft and slightly bitter, often eaten with maize porridge.
ranking.history: Morogo are wild leafy vegetables gathered by the peoples of southern Africa, growing abundantly in the rainy season. In the past, in seasons of food shortage, wild greens were an important source of nutrition, and women dried surplus greens to keep for the dry season. Today they remain a common side dish in Botswana households and also symbolize the traditional culture of gathering.

ranking.name: Magwinya (fat cakes)
ranking.description: Dough made from flour, yeast and sugar is deep-fried into round bread balls, crisp outside and soft inside, which can be eaten plain or filled with minced meat or jam.
ranking.history: Magwinya are common throughout southern Africa and similar to South Africa's 'vetkoek'; they are generally thought to originate from the fried-dough tradition of the Dutch and Afrikaners and to have reached Botswana after the spread of flour in the 19th century. Because they are simple to make and cheap, they are the most common breakfast and snack of street vendors and a source of small business for many women.
